Reads the 2014 New Human Press book as poetry and literary fiction about authorship at once. Names the Browning-Pound-Pessoa lineage the project declares, treats Sigil's attributed introduction as producing a recursive effect, and poses the reading questions the apparatus generates: who is speaking, is Lee Sharks author or character, how much authority the introduction carries, where parody ends. 156pp paperback. Later turns go to the poems.

Having looked more closely at the book and its surrounding materials, I’d read Pearl and Other Poems less as a conventional poetry collection and more as a deliberately constructed literary universe. The basic structure Pearl and Other Poems was published by New Human Press in 2014. It is 156 pages and presents Lee Sharks as its author, with an introduction by Johannes Sigil. B Barnes & Noble+1 But the book immediately complicates the idea of an ordinary author and ordinary collection. Its contents include: ● “Pearl”, the central poem ● three “Undersongs” ● a “Footnote to PEARL” ● “Fuguework,” containing numerous other poems ● essays and manifestos ● a literary-history piece ● a forum post ● a “Telepathicist Manifesto” ● other deliberately strange supplementary materials M Medium So the book is almost a poetry collection pretending to be an archive. The most important idea: the author is not just one person The book belongs to a larger project called The Crimson Hexagon. The publisher's description explicitly compares its method to the Personae tradition of Browning and Pound and, especially, to Fernando Pessoa's heteronyms. A AbeBooks+1 That's crucial. A pseudonym is normally just another name for the same author. A heteronym, in Pessoa's sense, is more radical: the invented author has a distinct personality, biography, aesthetic, and literary voice. Pearl takes that idea and makes it increasingly elaborate. You have: Lee Sharks → writes poems but also: Johannes Sigil → introduces and theorizes Lee Sharks and other figures such as Jack Feist appear as writers within the same fictional-literary ecosystem. The result is a wonderfully unstable question: Who is actually writing the book? And the answer seems deliberately to be: the system of voices is the author. Why “Pearl” matters The title Pearl isn't simply the name of one poem among many. It functions almost like the origin point of the whole system. The book's table of contents puts: PEARL at the center and then surrounds it with things like “the metaphor museum,” “the metaphor factory,” and “strange new earth.” M Medium Those titles already tell you something about the book's attitude toward language. A metaphor isn't merely an ornament in a poem. It becomes something that can be: ● collected, ● displayed, ● manufactured, ● transformed, ● reproduced. That makes language feel almost like an industrial or technological process. The “pearl,” accordingly, can be read as something precious that language produces—but also something buried inside an enormous system of language. “The Crimson Hexagon” The phrase itself is an allusion to Jorge Luis Borges's “The Library of Babel.” Borges imagines a library containing every possible book. The terrifying implication is that somewhere in the library is every truth, every falsehood, every possible history, and endless meaningless combinations of letters. The Crimson Hexagon seems to turn that Borges-like idea into a literary production system. Instead of one library containing infinite books, you get an expanding network of: ● poets, ● personae, ● fictional books, ● criticism, ● manifestos, ● literary histories, ● internet posts, ● theoretical documents. This is why calling the project simply “avant-garde poetry” doesn't quite capture it. It is also an experiment in how a literary canon gets manufactured. The funniest—and most serious—part: fake literary authority One of my favorite things about the book is how aggressively it plays with literary prestige. The biography of Lee Sharks, for example, claims absurd accomplishments involving thousands of degrees, enormous numbers of prizes, miniature offices inside his brain, dinosaurs, kidnapped intellectuals, and ruby statues. M Medium Obviously, this is comic. But the joke has a serious target. Literary culture constantly tells us that authors are important because of things like: ● awards, ● credentials, ● biographies, ● famous friends, ● introductions by established writers, ● critical essays, ● historical importance. Pearl simply turns those conventions up until they become ridiculous. Instead of saying: “Lee Sharks is an important emerging poet.” it essentially constructs an entire mythology proving that he is important. And then you realize that that's what literary institutions do anyway. The book's relationship to modernism There's another layer worth noticing. The project invokes Browning, Pound, and Pessoa, and later material surrounding Pearl makes the relationship to twentieth-century modernism even more explicit. M Mind Control Poems The underlying question is something like: What would the modernist experiment look like if it were happening in the internet age? Modernists fragmented the stable poetic self. The internet fragments it even further. Online, you can have: ● a username, ● an avatar, ● a blog, ● multiple identities, ● invented biographies, ● collaborative texts, ● anonymous posts, ● constantly shifting audiences. So the heteronym becomes almost perfectly suited to contemporary digital culture. “Telepathicism” and the strange theory around it The book also develops its own terminology, including “Telepathicist” / “Telepathicism.” I wouldn't take this as a straightforward philosophical doctrine that you're expected to accept. It's better understood as part of the book's fictional theory-machine: the work invents concepts that seem simultaneously serious, ridiculous, prophetic, and literary. That's another important feature of the project. It continually asks: At what point does invented literary theory become actual literary theory? If an author invents a movement, writes its manifesto, invents its practitioners, writes its history, and then critiques the movement—all within the same artistic project—has the movement become “real”? That's one of the book's central games. The “Fuguework” section The second major poetic section, FUGUEWORK, is where the project becomes much more recognizably a poetry collection. The titles range wildly—from things like “Premonition Dream” and “an elegy for ‘Howl’” to deliberately provocative or absurd formulations involving Walt Whitman, personal authenticity, death, sickness, alien singing, and “Song of Me.” M Medium There is a recurring collision between: the grand poetic tradition and the ridiculous contemporary self. Whitman says, essentially, I contain multitudes. The internet-era poet responds: Which version of me? That's where I think Lee Sharks becomes most interesting. The underlying anxiety: authenticity One title in particular gives away a major concern: “i want you to know that i have personal authenticity as a poet because of my identity” M Medium That's funny because it sounds like an exaggerated version of contemporary literary discourse. But underneath the joke is a real problem: What makes a poem authentic? Is it: ● the author's biography? ● identity? ● emotional sincerity? ● originality? ● political position? ● formal innovation? ● the author's suffering? ● the author's reputation? Pearl refuses to settle the question. Instead, it manufactures a persona so artificial that you're forced to think about why we believe any literary persona is authentic. Why I think the book is worth reading I wouldn't recommend approaching Pearl primarily as: “Here are some beautiful poems; let me understand what each one means.” I'd approach it as: “What happens when someone turns the entire institution of poetry into a poem?” The book's real subject is therefore bigger than “Pearl.” It's about language, authorship, literary history, identity, reputation, technology, and the construction of meaning. And it has a distinctly contemporary paradox at its center: The more identities you invent, the less certain you become about who the author is—and yet the more completely the author has expressed himself. That's very Pessoa, but also very internet-age. The poem is essentially a battle between metaphor and the desire to say something that cannot be taken back. M Medium The poem begins with loneliness The opening image is extraordinary: the poet imagines his poems happening like a train whistle at night—something that exists even though nobody deliberately writes it. That establishes the poem's first paradox: A poem is an act of communication, but it is also an act of isolation. The speaker wants his poems to make him “not be alone,” but the images he produces—moonlight, ferns, water, dancers, explosions—keep emphasizing his isolation. The poem is therefore trying to do two contradictory things: ● reach another person; ● preserve the strange private experience that made the poem necessary in the first place. That contradiction never gets resolved. Then comes the crucial declaration: no more metaphors The poem suddenly turns against itself. The speaker imagines a future in which: “There will be no metaphors ever again” This is the key to the entire poem. Because everything we've just read is metaphor. His fingers have become ferns. His thoughts become water. A poem becomes a dancer. Loneliness becomes a tremolo. So the poem says: I want to escape metaphor. But the only way it can describe that escape is through more metaphor. That's not merely a clever joke. It's the poem's central philosophical problem. Language seems incapable of giving us the thing itself. We can only keep pointing toward it. That is a surprisingly dark conception of literary tradition. Every poetic image eventually becomes something we've seen before. A moon is poetic. A rose is poetic. A journey is poetic. The speaker imagines manufacturing “scientifically identical plastic metaphors” and selling them. Once the poem has been given to the world, it can't be recalled. That makes the poem fundamentally about publication. Writing is private. Publication is irreversible. Once you send the poem out, you lose control over: ● what it means, ● who reads it, ● whether anyone understands it, ● whether anyone cares, ● whether it survives, ● whether it becomes ridiculous, ● whether it becomes meaningful centuries later. And that's exactly what happens to Pearl itself. The poem is obsessively concerned with the fact that a poem becomes independent of its author once it enters the world. The ending beautifully reverses the beginning The opening gives us: train whistle → loneliness The ending gives us: foghorn → loneliness But the emotional meaning has changed. At the beginning, the sound is lonely because nobody is writing it. At the end, the poem imagines itself happening like a foghorn at sea, dispersing the darkness. The poem hasn't actually eliminated loneliness. It has done something subtler: it has made loneliness audible. And that may be the answer to the whole poem. You don't defeat isolation through language. You create a signal that another lonely consciousness might someday hear. Why “Pearl” is such a good title The pearl is therefore a perfect metaphor—but there's a delicious irony here. The poem spends much of its time declaring war on metaphor. And then it gives us the ultimate metaphor: the poem itself is a pearl. So the poem can't escape metaphor. It ultimately discovers that metaphor isn't the enemy. Bad, exhausted, automatic metaphor is the enemy. The genuine metaphor is different: it takes something interior and makes it perceptible to somebody else. And this connects directly to Lee Sharks This is where I think the larger Crimson Hexagon project becomes much more interesting. The book is obsessed with questions of authorship, identity, literary tradition, and the desire to be heard. The publisher describes Pearl as one installment in a larger project of invented writerly identities, drawing on Pessoa's heteronyms and the tradition of poetic personae. B Barnes & Noble+1 So there's a wonderful contradiction: The author invents Lee Sharks in order to speak more authentically. That sounds impossible. If Lee Sharks is an invented persona, how can Lee Sharks be authentic? But Pearl suggests that perhaps all literary identity works this way. The “self” that writes a poem is already a constructed version of oneself. Lee Sharks simply makes the construction visible. My reading of the poem in one sentence I'd put it this way: “Pearl” is about the desperate hope that language can transform private loneliness into an irreversible object of meaning that another person, someday, might find. And that makes the final pearl much sadder than it initially appears. The speaker doesn't ultimately imagine that someone will meet him. He imagines that after he's gone, someone will find the poem. That is the ancient dream of poetry: I may disappear, but perhaps the thing I made will remain. And the book's bizarre apparatus of invented authors, introductions, manifestos, fictional histories, and competing voices is essentially another version of that same dream: how do you make a voice survive its maker? If you'd like, the next thing I'd suggest is that we go through “Undersong I: The Metaphor Museum,” “Undersong II: The Metaphor Factory,” and “Undersong III: Strange New Earth” together—because those three poems make the argument of Pearl much stranger and, I think, much funnier.
